\section{Interpretation, viable replacements, and scope}\label{sec:scope}

\subsection{The invalidated quantifier}

The theorem compares two statements that can look interchangeable but are
not.  A standalone plaquette factor has small tail
\[
  \frac{\int_{\dist(\one,V)\geq\rho}p_t(V)\,\dd V}
       {\int_Gp_t(V)\,\dd V}
  \xrightarrow[t\downarrow0]{}0.
\]
The interacting one-link kernel contains $m$ plaquette factors sharing the
same $U$.  Under the constructed boundary, the conditional probability that
the target plaquette is bad tends to one.  Thus ``typical under its own
factor'' cannot be replaced by ``typical uniformly under every microscopic
conditioning.''  The missing datum is the cost of producing the conditioning.

This conclusion is stable on a positive-measure boundary neighborhood, but
Theorem~\ref{thm:open-stability} intentionally does not estimate the marginal
probability of that neighborhood.  A successful global argument may show
that the frustrating neighborhood is rare and charge its rarity elsewhere.
The worst-boundary supremum prevents exactly that accounting.

\subsection{What remains viable}

Four broad replacements are untouched.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Restricted conditioning.}  One may prove a conditional estimate
only when a quantitative collar or boundary observable is coherent.  The
excluded boundaries must then be handled as defects rather than ignored.

\item \emph{Boundary averaging.}  Instead of a supremum, one may integrate
the conditional tail against the boundary marginal generated by the full
gauge measure.  The adverse boundary then carries its true action and entropy.

\item \emph{Block integration.}  Integrating several coupled links before
defining a defect can turn the frustrated compromise into an internal block
cost.  Theorem~\ref{thm:dobrushin-failure} concerns single-link coordinates
and does not constrain a block Dobrushin matrix.

\item \emph{Labeled contours or polymers.}  A connected object can record the
central or geometric charge responsible for a bad plaquette and include the
supporting boundary links in its activity.  Such a construction must prove
its own energy--entropy and overlap bounds; none is supplied here.
\end{enumerate}

These alternatives express a common principle: dependence is not removed by
conditioning; it is relocated to the conditioned data.  A representation
that exposes a local plaquette defect while forgetting the charge in its
boundary cannot support a boundary-uniform rarity statement.

\subsection{Formal limitations}

All results are at fixed finite lattice spacing and finite volume.  The heat
time tends to zero, but no lattice spacing is introduced and no continuum
limit is taken.  The action is the heat-kernel plaquette action, not the
Wilson action; an extension to other actions would require a uniform
small-parameter rate theorem.  The central construction applies only when
$G$ has a nonidentity center.  The Dobrushin statement uses total variation
on raw link variables and does not cover gauge-reduced or block metrics.

There is no claim of confinement, infinite-volume phase coexistence,
reflection positivity in a limit, Osterwalder--Schrader reconstruction,
Hamiltonian spectral information, or a mass gap.  In particular, a finite
conditional concentration scale is not a physical particle mass.  Relative
to the four-dimensional Yang--Mills existence and mass-gap problem, the
paper is a restricted finite-lattice obstruction theorem: it removes one
candidate proof quantifier and leaves the construction problem open.
